chapter_title: Design of Micropiles for Structure Foundations

sections.title: Introduction and Design Overview
sections.body: This chapter presents the design methodology for micropiles used as directly loaded structural elements (CASE 1 micropiles). The design procedure follows a 12-step process outlined in Table 5-1, supplemented by 8 additional design considerations including corrosion protection, plunge length, end bearing, downdrag, lateral loading, buckling, and seismic considerations. The design approach covers both structural (internal) and geotechnical (external) limit states. The structural design ensures that the micropile cross section has adequate capacity to resist the applied loads, while the geotechnical design ensures that the surrounding ground can develop sufficient resistance through grout-to-ground bond. The 12 design steps are: (1) evaluate feasibility, (2) review available geotechnical data, (3) determine loading conditions, (4) prepare preliminary design, (5) structural design of cased length, (6) structural design of uncased length, (7) revise design, (8) estimate geotechnical capacity, (9) estimate settlement, (10) design pile cap connections, (11) determine load testing requirements, and (12) prepare drawings and specifications.

sections.title: Structural Design of Cased Length
sections.body: The cased length of the micropile is the portion where both the steel casing and grout (and optionally a center reinforcing bar) are present. The structural design of the cased length involves checking three conditions: (1) compression capacity, (2) tension capacity, and (3) combined axial load and bending. For compression (Eq. 5-1), the allowable load is the sum of contributions from the grout, casing, and center bar: P_c-allowable = 0.40*f'c_grout*A_grout + 0.47*F_y-steel*(A_bar + A_casing). For tension (Eq. 5-2), the allowable load is: P_t-allowable = 0.55*F_y-steel*(A_bar + A_casing). No tensile contribution from grout is considered. For combined axial and bending (Eq. 5-3), the interaction check uses: f_a/F_a + f_b/F_b <= 1.0, where f_a is the computed axial stress, F_a is the allowable axial stress, f_b is the computed bending stress, and F_b is the allowable bending stress. Section properties are computed using composite section analysis. The moment of inertia of the cased section (Eq. 5-4a) is: I_composite = (pi/64)*[(OD^4 - ID^4) + n_bar*(d_bar^4) + (n_grout - 1)*((ID - 2*cover)^4)], where n is the modular ratio. The section modulus (Eq. 5-4b) is S = I_composite/(OD/2). The radius of gyration (Eq. 5-4c) is r = sqrt(I_composite/A_composite). Factors of 0.40 and 0.47 are AASHTO allowable stress factors for grout and steel, respectively.

sections.title: Buckling and Stability of Cased Length
sections.body: For micropiles that extend through air, water, or very weak soils, the cased length must be checked for Euler buckling. The Euler buckling load (Eq. 5-5) is: P_critical = pi^2*E*I / (K*L_unsupported)^2, where E is the modulus of elasticity, I is the moment of inertia of the steel casing, K is the effective length factor (typically 1.0 for pinned-pinned or 2.0 for cantilever), and L_unsupported is the unsupported length. The Richards and Rothbauer (2004) method provides an alternative approach (Eq. 5-6) that accounts for the lateral support provided by surrounding soil using subgrade reaction theory. The allowable axial stress in compression should be reduced when buckling is a concern, using the AASHTO column formula approach. In general, buckling is not a concern for micropiles that are fully embedded in soil or rock with adequate lateral support. However, buckling should be evaluated when micropiles pass through very weak or liquefiable soils, through voids (karstic terrain), or above ground/water level.

sections.title: Structural Design of Uncased Length
sections.body: The uncased length (bond zone) of the micropile is the portion where the grout and center reinforcing bar (without steel casing) transfer load to the ground through grout-to-ground bond. The structural design of the uncased length checks compression and tension capacity of the grout-bar cross section. For compression (Eq. 5-7): P_c-allowable = 0.40*f'c_grout*A_grout + 0.47*F_y-steel*A_bar. For tension (Eq. 5-8): P_t-allowable = 0.55*F_y-steel*A_bar. Only the center reinforcing bar contributes to tensile capacity in the uncased length. The grout diameter in the uncased length is typically equal to the drilled hole diameter, which may be larger than the casing outside diameter depending on drilling method and ground conditions. If the micropile design includes a plunge length (Section 5.15), the load reaching the uncased length is reduced by the transfer load developed over the plunge length.

sections.title: Geotechnical Capacity - Grout-to-Ground Bond
sections.body: The geotechnical capacity of a micropile is controlled by the grout-to-ground bond developed along the micropile bond zone. The ultimate bond resistance (Eq. 5-9) is: R_bond = alpha_bond * pi * D_b * L_bond, where alpha_bond is the unit grout-to-ground bond stress, D_b is the bond zone diameter, and L_bond is the bond length. The allowable geotechnical capacity (Eq. 5-10) is: P_G-allowable = R_bond / FS, where FS is the factor of safety (typically 2.0 to 2.5 for micropile bond). Table 5-3 provides presumptive values of alpha_bond for various soil and rock types and grouting methods (Types A, B, C, D). For Type A grouting in rock, alpha_bond ranges from 345 to 4150 kPa depending on rock quality. For Type B grouting in sand, alpha_bond ranges from 70 to 360 kPa. For Type B grouting in clay, alpha_bond ranges from 25 to 190 kPa. Higher bond values are achieved with Type C and D grouting. These values are presumptive and should be verified by site-specific load testing. For critical projects, the designer should specify verification load testing to confirm the achievable bond values for the specific site conditions and contractor methods.

sections.title: Group Capacity and Efficiency
sections.body: When micropiles are installed in groups, group effects may reduce the capacity of individual piles due to overlapping stress zones. The group efficiency factor (Eq. 5-11) is defined as the ratio of the ultimate group capacity to the sum of the individual pile ultimate capacities. For axial loading, group effects for micropiles are generally similar to those for conventional piles. Table 5-4 provides group efficiency factors based on center-to-center spacing. For micropile spacings of 3 diameters or more, group efficiency is typically 1.0 (no reduction). Block failure of the micropile group must also be evaluated. For compression block failure (Eq. 5-12), the ultimate group capacity is: Q_group = min(sum of individual capacities, block perimeter bond capacity + base bearing). For uplift block failure (Eq. 5-16/5-17), the ultimate uplift capacity is: Q_uplift = min(sum of individual uplift capacities, block weight + side resistance). Punching failure into a weak underlying layer should be checked using Eq. 5-15. The group capacity is the minimum of the individual pile capacity sum (reduced by efficiency factor) and the block failure capacity.

sections.title: Settlement Estimation
sections.body: Settlement of micropile foundations must be estimated and compared to tolerable limits. Settlement of a single micropile or group includes two components: (1) elastic compression of the micropile element itself, and (2) settlement of the surrounding ground due to load transfer. The elastic compression (Eq. 5-18) of the micropile is: delta_elastic = P*L / (A*E), where P is the applied load, L is the length, A is the cross-sectional area, and E is the composite modulus. For a micropile group, the settlement is estimated using conventional methods for deep foundations. Meyerhof (1976) proposed that the settlement of a pile group in sand can be estimated as (Eq. 5-19): s_group = 0.92*q*sqrt(B_g) / N_corr, where q is the applied stress, B_g is the group width, and N_corr is the corrected SPT N value. For pile groups in clay, conventional consolidation theory is applied using the equivalent footing method where the load is assumed to act on an equivalent footing located at 2/3 of the bond length depth. Additional settlement equations (Eq. 5-20 through 5-22) address elastic shortening of the micropile under the applied load considering the composite section stiffness and load transfer distribution along the bond zone.

sections.title: Pile Cap Connections
sections.body: The connection between the micropile and the pile cap (or existing footing for underpinning) must be designed to transfer the applied loads from the structure to the micropile. Various connection details are used depending on whether the micropile is a new installation or an underpinning element. For new construction, the micropile casing is typically embedded a minimum of 150 mm (6 inches) into the pile cap, and the center reinforcing bar extends into the cap with adequate development length. Connection details include: (1) flush-mounted casing with reinforcing bar extending into the cap, (2) casing with welded bearing plate, (3) casing with mechanical connector to the cap reinforcement, and (4) threaded bar with plate and nut bearing on the cap surface. For underpinning, micropiles are typically installed by coring through the existing footing and grouting the micropile into the cored hole. The cored hole provides confinement and load transfer through grout-to-concrete bond. The bearing plate connection is commonly used for micropiles designed to carry tension loads, where a torqued anchor plate at the top of the micropile engages the pile cap. Figures 5-10 through 5-16 illustrate various connection details for both new and retrofit applications.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection
sections.body: Corrosion protection for micropiles must be evaluated based on the aggressiveness of the ground environment and the loading conditions (tension vs. compression). Table 5-5 defines aggressive ground conditions as soils with pH less than 4.5, resistivity less than 2000 ohm-cm, sulfate concentration greater than 200 ppm, or chloride concentration greater than 100 ppm. Table 5-6 provides corrosion protection recommendations for micropiles differentiated by loading (tension vs. compression) and ground aggressiveness. For casings in compression in aggressive ground, a minimum section loss of 1.6 mm (0.063 in.) on the outside is prescribed per AASHTO Section 4.5.7.4. For core steel (reinforcing bar) in tension in aggressive ground, the recommended protection includes: epoxy coating, galvanization, or encapsulation in plastic sheath, plus minimum grout cover (1 inch in soil, 0.5 inch in rock). Corrosion protection must extend 5 m (15 ft) below corrosive material. Double corrosion protection (as shown in Figure 5-17 for GEWI piles) uses a corrugated sheath between the bar and grout with inner cement grout filling the annulus. For permanent micropiles in tension, double corrosion protection is recommended in aggressive environments.

sections.title: Plunge Length and End Bearing
sections.body: The casing plunge length is the portion of the steel casing that extends into the bond zone below the cased/uncased transition (see Figure 5-18). The plunge length allows a portion of the applied load to be transferred to the ground through grout-to-ground bond along the cased section, reducing the load that must be carried by the uncased bond zone. The allowable transfer load (Eq. 5-25) is: P_transfer-allowable = (alpha_bond / FS) * pi * D_b * Plunge_Length, where alpha_bond is from Table 5-3. The use of plunge length to reduce load on the uncased section should be verified by load testing. Regarding end bearing, micropiles are typically designed as friction (bond) piles, and end bearing is generally considered negligible due to the small cross-sectional area. However, micropiles founded on high-quality sound rock may develop their capacity primarily through end bearing. For end bearing on rock, a nominal rock socket length of approximately 0.6 m (2 ft) is typically used to verify that the micropile is founded on competent rock. Table 5-2 provides minimum rock quality criteria for end bearing micropiles. The capacity of end bearing micropiles on competent rock is typically controlled by the structural capacity of the micropile rather than the geotechnical resistance.

sections.title: Downdrag on Micropiles
sections.body: Micropiles may be subjected to additional axial compression loading from downdrag (negative skin friction) when soils in contact with the cased portion settle relative to the micropile. Downdrag potential exists when: (1) the site is underlain by compressible silts, clays, or peats; (2) fill has been recently placed; or (3) the groundwater has been substantially lowered. The maximum load along the micropile occurs at the top of the bond zone and equals the sum of the applied load at the pile top plus the downdrag force. To compute the downdrag force, the grout-to-ground bond stress values from Table 5-3 are used over the length of the micropile in the settling soils. The structural capacity of the micropile must be checked for this maximum load (applied load + downdrag). The small surface area of micropiles results in relatively small downdrag forces compared to larger diameter piles. Further isolation from downdrag can be achieved by installing an additional oversized outer casing through the settling soils. Battered micropiles should not be used at sites with large soil settlements because of additional bending forces.

sections.title: Design for Lateral Loading - Single Micropiles
sections.body: The design of micropiles for lateral loading uses p-y analysis methods similar to those for conventional piles. The analysis of a single vertical micropile under lateral loading is equivalent to that for a driven pile or drilled shaft using programs such as LPILE. The design procedure involves 7 steps: (1) determine pile parameters including length, modulus of elasticity, and distance from pile head to ground surface; (2) divide the micropile into segments with uniform cross-sectional properties (cased vs. uncased); (3) delineate the soil/rock profile over the anticipated penetration depth; (4) determine soil parameters for each layer including unit weight, shear strength, epsilon_50 for clays, and soil modulus k; (5) determine critical loading combinations and boundary conditions; (6) evaluate structural capacity for combined axial and lateral loading using Eq. 5-3 or 5-6; (7) check deflection acceptability. Tables 5-7 through 5-10 provide soil parameters for p-y analysis: epsilon_50 values for intact clays (Table 5-7), epsilon_50 for stiff clays (Table 5-8), k values for sands (Table 5-9), and k values for clays (Table 5-10). Table 5-11 provides guidance on pile head fixity for micropile-footing connections: 0% fixity (pinned) for 300 mm casing embedment, 50% fixity for 450 mm embedment, and 100% fixity (fixed) for 600 mm or greater embedment. The bending moment capacity at threaded casing joints should be evaluated using Eq. 5-26 (reduced section modulus at joint) and Eq. 5-27 (maximum moment at joint location).

sections.title: Lateral Resistance of Micropile Groups
sections.body: Micropile behavior in a group configuration under lateral loading is influenced by pile-soil-pile interaction. Piles in trailing rows have less resistance to lateral load than piles in the lead row, resulting in a group efficiency less than 1.0. The p-multiplier concept (Pm) is used to modify p-y curves for individual piles to account for group effects. Based on Brown et al. (1998) and the FOREVER project, recommended p-multiplier values for micropile groups at 3-diameter spacing are: 0.8 for the front (lead) row, 0.4 for the second row, and 0.3 for the third and subsequent rows. For in-line micropiles, group effects are negligible for spacing between 6 to 7 diameters. For micropiles perpendicular to loading direction, group effects are negligible for spacing greater than 3 diameters. The 5-step design procedure for laterally loaded micropile groups is: (1) develop p-y curves for single pile; (2) perform LPILE analyses using Pm values for each row position; (3) estimate group deflection under lateral load; (4) evaluate structural acceptability by checking maximum bending moment; (5) perform refined evaluation considering superstructure-substructure interaction. Soil-structure interaction programs such as FB-Pier and GROUP can be used for detailed group analysis.

sections.title: Buckling Considerations for Micropiles
sections.body: Buckling of micropiles is a concern when piles pass through very weak or liquefiable soils, through voids (karstic terrain), or where the pile extends above ground. For micropiles surrounded by very weak or liquefiable soil, the critical buckling load (Eq. 5-28) is: P_cr = pi^2*E*I/l^2 + E_s*l^2/pi^2, where E is the casing steel modulus, I is the moment of inertia, l is the unsupported length, and E_s is the lateral reaction modulus of the soil. The limiting lateral reaction modulus for buckling (Eq. 5-29) is: E_s_LIMIT = 1 / [(4*I/A^2) * (E/Fy^2)], which defines the pile factor as the product of geometric (4I/A^2) and material (E/Fy^2) terms. If E_s_LIMIT is less than the actual E_s, buckling does not control. Tables 5-12 and 5-13 provide ranges of E_s values for various soil types (by soil type and by SPT N value, respectively). Figure 5-23 provides a chart of limiting lateral modulus values for various micropile materials. When buckling potential exists (E_s_LIMIT > E_s), the allowable compression load is modified using Eq. 5-30, with the allowable stress Fa computed from Eq. 5-31 or 5-32 depending on the slenderness ratio Kl/r relative to the critical slenderness Cc. For micropiles installed through voids (Section 5.20.3), the unsupported length equals the void thickness, and the effective length factor K depends on end conditions (pinned-pinned K=1.0 is conservative). The moment of inertia at casing joints should be used for evaluating buckling through joints (I_joint from Eq. 5-26).

sections.title: Seismic Considerations
sections.body: Micropiles used in seismic regions must be designed to resist earthquake-induced forces including increased axial loads from overturning, lateral loads from inertial forces, and potential effects of soil liquefaction. The seismic response of a micropile foundation involves three-dimensional soil-pile interaction with axial (t-z curves), lateral (p-y curves), and torsional components. Design considerations include: (1) use of battered micropiles to resist horizontal seismic deformations, noting that vertical micropiles provide limited lateral resistance due to their relatively low stiffness; (2) evaluation of pile uplift capacity under seismic overturning with FS = 1.0 per AASHTO for uplift from seismic forces; (3) load sharing between existing and new foundations for retrofit applications; (4) increased pile cap reinforcement to ensure ductile foundation response (reinforcement ratio rho_s of about 0.5% achieves fully ductile response per Trinh et al., 2004); and (5) evaluation of liquefaction effects including reduced lateral support (0.1 to 1.0% of non-liquefied resistance per Ishihara and Cubrinovski, 1998). Battered micropiles are effective at reducing pore pressure buildup and limiting seismically-induced soil movements in the zone around the piles (FOREVER, 2003). However, battered micropiles should not be used where ground settlement around the pile is expected due to additional bending forces.

sections.title: Load Testing Requirements
sections.body: Load testing of micropiles is essential to verify the design assumptions, particularly the grout-to-ground bond stress values. Two types of load tests are used: (1) verification (or proof) tests performed on sacrificial micropiles to confirm the ultimate capacity, and (2) proof tests performed on production micropiles to confirm acceptable performance at the design load. For verification testing, the micropile is loaded to a minimum of 2.0 times the design load (Eq. 5-23). The ultimate geotechnical capacity (Eq. 5-24) is determined from the load-displacement curve as the load at which the micropile displacement is excessive or the load-displacement curve shows a distinct break. Acceptance criteria typically require that creep (sustained loading) at 1.5 times the design load does not exceed specified limits, and that the elastic displacement at the maximum test load is consistent with the expected elastic shortening of the micropile. Both compression and tension load tests should be performed, as the bond behavior may differ under different loading conditions. A minimum of 2 to 5 percent of production micropiles should be proof tested.
